country.name: Canada
country.tagline: A cold-climate wine country that turned its hardest winters into icewine, and is now learning to make Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc to match.

stats.note: Approximate national totals from 2015 industry figures (Wikipedia, Canadian wine: 12,150 ha, 56 million litres, 548 wineries). Updates: Ontario about 13,600 acres in the Niagara Peninsula alone (OWAA 2024 to 2025); BC 8,686 insured wine-grape acres in 2026 (BC Ministry of Agriculture, July 2026). OIV does not list Canada among major producers; it records Canadian consumption of 2.8 mhl in 2025.

country.overview:
Canada grows wine grapes in four main provinces: Ontario and British Columbia make nearly all of it, with smaller and fast-growing industries in Quebec and Nova Scotia. Almost every Canadian vineyard sits within a few kilometres of a large body of water (Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, Okanagan Lake, the Bay of Fundy, the St. Lawrence), because water is what makes viticulture possible this far north. Lakes store summer heat, slow spring budbreak until frost danger has passed, and soften the deep winter cold that can kill vines.

That cold is also Canada's signature. Canada is the world's largest producer of icewine, made from grapes left to freeze on the vine and picked at minus 8 degrees Celsius or below; about 90 percent of it comes from Ontario. Inniskillin's 1989 Vidal icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux in 1991 and announced Canada to the wine world. Since then, the quality wines have shifted toward dry styles: Niagara Chardonnay, Riesling and Cabernet Franc; Prince Edward County Pinot Noir grown on limestone; Okanagan Merlot, Syrah and Bordeaux blends from desert benches; Quebec hybrids; Nova Scotia's crisp Tidal Bay whites and traditional-method sparkling.

Canada's appellation system is provincial, not federal. Ontario and British Columbia use the Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA): wines must be made entirely from grapes grown in the province and pass a tasting panel, and appellation names carry minimum-origin rules. Quebec has protected geographical indications (IGP Vin du Québec, plus IGPs for icewine and ice cider), and Nova Scotia has its Tidal Bay appellation. A long-running anomaly is 'International-Canadian Blends' (formerly 'Cellared in Canada'), wines bottled in Canada largely from imported bulk wine, which outsell VQA wine on many shelves.

Recent years have been hard. Deep freezes in December 2022 and January 2024 destroyed most of the Okanagan's 2024 crop and forced growers to pull and replant thousands of acres. In 2025, US tariffs prompted Canadian provinces to remove American wine from liquor-board shelves, a sudden opening for domestic producers.

history.title: Vinland
history.text: Norse sagas name the land Leif Erikson reached 'Vinland' for its wild grapes or berries; L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is the only confirmed Norse site.

history.title: Johann Schiller at Cooksville
history.text: Johann Schiller, a German-born former soldier, is said to have made wine from wild and domesticated labrusca vines on the Credit River west of Toronto around 1811; he is often called the father of Canadian wine. The Comte de Courtenay later expanded the vineyard as Clair House, which showed wine in Paris in 1867.

history.title: Father Pandosy's mission vineyard
history.text: Oblate missionary Charles Pandosy plants vines at his mission near present-day Kelowna to make sacramental wine, the first in the Okanagan.

history.title: Vin Villa on Pelee Island
history.text: Kentucky planters found Vin Villa on Pelee Island in Lake Erie, Canada's first commercial winery.

history.title: Prohibition and the licence freeze
history.text: Provincial prohibition (Ontario 1916 to 1927) exempted native wine, so wineries multiplied; afterward Ontario's Liquor Control Board froze new winery licences, and none was issued in Niagara from 1929 until 1975.

history.title: Inniskillin
history.text: Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser receive the first new Ontario winery licence since 1929 and found Inniskillin at Niagara-on-the-Lake.

history.title: Free trade and the VQA
history.text: The 1988 Canada-US Free Trade Agreement removes protection for Canadian wine; growers are paid to pull out labrusca and hybrid vines and replant vinifera. Ontario launches the voluntary VQA in 1988 and BC follows in 1990.

history.title: Icewine at Vinexpo
history.text: Inniskillin 1989 Vidal Icewine wins the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux, Canada's first major international wine award.

history.title: VQA becomes law; EU opens to icewine
history.text: Ontario's VQA Act (1999) makes VQA the provincial wine authority; in 2001 the EU accepts Canadian icewine standards and allows imports.

history.title: Sub-appellations in BC
history.text: Golden Mile Bench becomes BC's first sub-GI (2015); Okanagan Falls, Naramata Bench, Skaha Bench and others follow, and six more are added in June 2022.

history.title: The Okanagan freeze
history.text: A January 2024 cold snap, after damage in December 2022, destroys nearly the whole 2024 Okanagan crop; most damaged acres are replanted by 2026.

country.classification: Canada has no federal appellation system; wine origin is a provincial matter. Ontario: VQA Ontario (Vintners Quality Alliance Act, 1999) recognises three primary appellations (Niagara Peninsula, Lake Erie North Shore, Prince Edward County), two regional appellations within the Niagara Peninsula (Niagara-on-the-Lake and Niagara Escarpment) and 11 sub-appellations (10 in Niagara plus South Islands). VQA wines must be 100 percent Ontario-grown, at least 85 percent from a named appellation, and pass laboratory and tasting tests. British Columbia: BC VQA and the BC Wine Authority recognise the British Columbia GI, nine regional GIs and 12 sub-GIs (11 in the Okanagan plus Cowichan Valley); wines naming a GI need at least 95 percent of grapes from it. Icewine everywhere must come from grapes naturally frozen on the vine, picked at minus 8 degrees Celsius or colder, with at least 35 degrees Brix. Quebec: the IGP Vin du Québec covers wines from 100 percent Quebec grapes; separate IGPs protect Vin de glace du Québec and Cidre de glace du Québec. Nova Scotia: Tidal Bay is a provincial appellation-style designation for blended whites. 'International-Canadian Blends' may contain mostly imported wine.
country.climate_soils: Short, warm growing seasons and dangerous winters. Niagara and Lake Erie North Shore rely on the Great Lakes and on the Niagara Escarpment, which traps lake air against the benches; soils are glacial clays, silts and limestone-derived tills. Prince Edward County has shallow clay loam over fractured limestone, and growers often bury vines under soil for winter. The southern Okanagan is the northern tip of the Sonoran-type desert ecosystem, with under 300 mm of rain and very hot days; glacial benches of sand and gravel. Quebec's continental winters force hybrids and protective covers; Nova Scotia is cool and maritime.

grapes.name: Vidal Blanc
grapes.note: Thick-skinned hybrid that is the backbone of Ontario icewine.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Niagara's most consistent dry and icewine variety.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Niagara benches and Prince Edward County; the focus of the i4C cool-climate Chardonnay festival.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: Ontario's best red and an icewine grape.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Prince Edward County, Niagara, Okanagan Kelowna area and Vancouver Island.

grapes.name: L'Acadie Blanc
grapes.note: Hybrid bred at Vineland, Ontario, now Nova Scotia's signature grape.

regions.name: Ontario
regions.tagline: Lake-moderated vineyards on the Niagara benches, Lake Erie's warm shore and Prince Edward County's limestone.
regions.summary: Ontario makes about 60 percent of Canadian wine from about 17,000 acres (6,900 ha) of vines in three appellations between 41 and 44 degrees north, the same latitude band as Tuscany and Oregon but with far colder winters. Niagara Peninsula is the heart (105 wineries and 13,600 acres in 2024 to 2025); Lake Erie North Shore is the warmest; Prince Edward County is the coldest and most terroir-obsessed. Ontario produces about 90 percent of Canada's icewine.
regions.history: Johann Schiller's Credit River vineyard (around 1811) and Pelee Island's Vin Villa (1866) were the first. T.G. Bright and Company (1874) became a giant of sweet, fortified 'port' and 'sherry' from labrusca. Prohibition (1916 to 1927) exempted Ontario wine, and dozens of wineries sprang up; the Liquor Control Board then froze licences. Inniskillin's 1975 licence and Château des Charmes (1978, Paul Bosc, first all-vinifera estate in Niagara) began the modern era; VQA followed in 1988.
regions.terroir: Lake Ontario and the 'lake effect' along the Niagara Escarpment, Lake Erie's shallow, warm water, and the limestone of Prince Edward County. Glacial lake beds (Lake Iroquois) left benches of clay, silt and dolomitic limestone-derived soils.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Vidal, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: Icewine; dry and off-dry Riesling; mineral Chardonnay; Cabernet Franc; Gamay; traditional-method sparkling.
regions.classification: VQA Ontario: three primary appellations, two regional appellations, 11 sub-appellations.

regions.name: Niagara Peninsula
regions.tagline: Canada's largest wine region, squeezed between Lake Ontario and the Niagara Escarpment.
regions.summary: The Niagara Peninsula appellation runs about 55 km from Grimsby to the Niagara River. The Niagara Escarpment, a limestone cliff that continues to Niagara Falls, traps air off Lake Ontario: in spring the cool lake delays budbreak, in autumn the warm lake delays frost, and on winter nights air circulating along the escarpment keeps the benches warmer than the plain. The appellation averages about 1,590 growing degree days (Celsius). Ten sub-appellations, grouped into two regional appellations, divide benchland from lakeshore plain.
regions.history: Inniskillin (1975), Château des Charmes (1978) and Cave Spring (1986) proved vinifera could thrive here. Tawse, Hidden Bench, Le Clos Jordanne (Burgundian collaboration with Boisset, 2003 to 2012, revived by Arterra) and Southbrook (biodynamic) define the modern style.
regions.terroir: Benchlands of the escarpment: limestone, dolomite and shale-derived clays, well drained, with cooling breezes. Lake plain: deeper, heavier clay and silt over the old Lake Iroquois bed, warmer and earlier ripening near the lake.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Vidal.
regions.styles: Bench Riesling and Chardonnay; Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux blends from Niagara-on-the-Lake; icewine.
regions.classification: Niagara Peninsula appellation; regional appellations Niagara-on-the-Lake (four sub-appellations) and Niagara Escarpment (three); three other sub-appellations (Creek Shores, Lincoln Lakeshore, Vinemount Ridge).

regions.name: British Columbia
regions.tagline: Desert benches above glacial lakes, island vineyards and mountain valleys at the edge of viable viticulture.
regions.summary: British Columbia has around 10,000 acres of wine grapes and more than 300 wineries, most of them small. The Okanagan Valley holds about 90 percent of the vineyards and 95 percent of output; the rest are in the Similkameen, on Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, in the Fraser Valley and in the new interior GIs (Thompson Valley, Shuswap, Lillooet, Kootenays). In 2026 the top varieties by insured acreage were Pinot Noir, Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Gris and Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.history: Father Pandosy planted mission vines near Kelowna in 1859; Calona Wines (1932) is BC's oldest continuously operating winery. After the 1988 Free Trade Agreement growers pulled out most of their hybrid vineyards with government help and replanted with vinifera, and BC VQA began in 1990. Nk'Mip Cellars (2002), owned by the Osoyoos Indian Band, is often cited as the first Indigenous-owned winery in North America. Cold snaps in December 2022 and January 2024 destroyed nearly the whole 2024 crop, forcing about 1,970 acres to be removed in 2025, almost all of them replanted in 2026.
regions.terroir: Glacial terraces (benches) of sand, gravel and silt above long, deep lakes; the south is semi-arid with under 300 mm of rain, very hot summer days and cool nights. Winter lows below minus 20 degrees Celsius are the main hazard.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Merlot, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Riesling, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style blends and Syrah from the south Okanagan; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling from the north and the coast; icewine.
regions.classification: BC Wine Authority: British Columbia GI, nine regional GIs, 12 sub-GIs (wines naming a GI need 95 percent of grapes from it).

regions.name: Okanagan Valley
regions.tagline: A 200 km string of lakes from the Sonoran-edge desert at Osoyoos to the cool orchards of Lake Country.
regions.summary: The Okanagan Valley GI runs about 175 km north to south along a chain of glacial lakes (Okanagan, Skaha, Vaseux, Osoyoos). The south around Oliver and Osoyoos is the hottest, driest corner of Canada, where the Black Sage Bench and Golden Mile Bench grow Merlot, Cabernet, Syrah and Malbec; the north around Kelowna and Lake Country is cooler and suits Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and sparkling wine. Eleven sub-GIs subdivide it (Golden Mile Bench 2015; Okanagan Falls 2018; Naramata Bench and Skaha Bench 2019; Golden Mile Slopes; six more in 2022).
regions.history: Pandosy's 1859 mission vineyard, Calona (1932), the post-1988 vinifera replanting, and an explosion of estate wineries after 2000 (Mission Hill, Burrowing Owl, Quails' Gate, Osoyoos Larose, Painted Rock, Blue Mountain).
regions.terroir: Glacial benches of sand, gravel and silt, alluvial fans and some granite; large lakes moderate temperatures; rainfall below 250 mm near Osoyoos to about 400 mm in the north.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Gewürztraminer.
regions.styles: From ripe Bordeaux blends and Syrah to taut Pinot Noir, Riesling and sparkling.

regions.name: Quebec
regions.tagline: Hybrids under winter blankets, and the birthplace of ice cider.
regions.summary: Quebec's wine industry is young, cold and fast-growing, concentrated south of Montreal in Montérégie and the Eastern Townships (Brome-Missisquoi around Dunham is the historic heart), with vineyards also near Quebec City and on Île d'Orléans. Winters reach minus 30 degrees Celsius, so growers rely on cold-hardy hybrids (Frontenac, Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix) or protect vinifera by hilling soil over the trunks and covering rows with geotextile fabric. The IGP Vin du Québec requires 100 percent Quebec grapes.
regions.history: Jacques Cartier found wild vines on Île d'Orléans in 1535 and called it Île de Bacchus; Samuel de Champlain's European vines died in 1608. The modern industry began in the early 1980s around Dunham: Christian Barthomeuf planted Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise in 1980, and L'Orpailleur was founded in 1982. Barthomeuf also created ice cider (cidre de glace) around 1989, now a Quebec speciality with its own IGP.
regions.terroir: Glacial and slate-derived soils in the Appalachian foothills; continental climate with hot summers, short seasons and severe winters.
regions.grapes: Frontenac (noir, gris, blanc), Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir under cover.
regions.styles: Crisp whites, rosé, light reds, icewine, ice cider.
regions.classification: IGP Vin du Québec; IGP Vin de glace du Québec; IGP Cidre de glace du Québec.

Wikipedia: Quebec wine

regions.name: Nova Scotia
regions.tagline: Tidal valleys on the Bay of Fundy, crisp whites and world-class sparkling wine.
regions.summary: Nova Scotia has a few hundred hectares of vines and around 20 to 30 wineries, mostly in the Annapolis and Gaspereau valleys near the Bay of Fundy, whose enormous tides moderate temperatures. The province's identity rests on two styles: Tidal Bay, a crisp, low-alcohol blended white appellation (first vintage 2012), and traditional-method sparkling wine, led by Benjamin Bridge. L'Acadie Blanc, a hybrid bred in Ontario, is the signature grape.
regions.history: Governor Isaac de Razilly wrote in 1634 that 'Bordeaux vines' were doing well at La Hève (LaHave); the Acadians grew grapes in the 17th century. Roger Dial founded Grand Pré Winery in 1979; Jost Vineyards (1983) at Malagash followed.
regions.terroir: Cool maritime climate, short season; soils of sandstone, shale and glacial till.
regions.grapes: L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Geisenheim 318, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Marechal Foch, Lucie Kuhlmann.
regions.styles: Tidal Bay white blends; traditional-method sparkling; fruit wines.
regions.classification: Tidal Bay appellation (provincial standard, tasting panel approval).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nova Scotia wine

ca-beamsville-bench.name: Beamsville Bench
ca-beamsville-bench.summary: The western escarpment bench around Beamsville, with steep, northward-facing slopes, well-drained clay-loam over dolomitic limestone and the most frost-free days on the escarpment (about 217); 12 wineries. Known for taut Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

ca-cidre-de-glace-du-quebec.name: Cidre de glace du Québec
ca-cidre-de-glace-du-quebec.summary: Quebec's IGP for ice cider, made from apples or apple juice concentrated by natural winter cold. Christian Barthomeuf of Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise is credited with inventing it around 1989; Domaine Pinnacle and La Face Cachée de la Pomme made it famous. Not a grape wine, but a Quebec signature alongside icewine.
producers: La Face Cachée de la Pomme

ca-cowichan-valley.name: Cowichan Valley
ca-cowichan-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega, Chardonnay
ca-cowichan-valley.summary: Vancouver Island's sub-GI, a warm pocket north of Victoria (its name is said to mean 'warm land' in Hul'q'umi'num). Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and sparkling wine from small family wineries.

ca-creek-shores.name: Creek Shores
ca-creek-shores.summary: A lakeshore-plain sub-appellation between St. Catharines and Jordan, crossed by creeks (Twenty Mile, Fifteen Mile, Sixteen Mile) that drain the escarpment; about 1,550 growing degree days. Lake Ontario and the creeks moderate temperatures.

ca-east-kelowna-slopes.name: East Kelowna Slopes
ca-east-kelowna-slopes.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
ca-east-kelowna-slopes.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 2,900 ha in the hills east of Kelowna, higher and cooler, home to Tantalus, whose old-vine Riesling comes from vines planted in 1978.

ca-four-mile-creek.name: Four Mile Creek
ca-four-mile-creek.summary: Sub-appellation on the flat plain of Niagara-on-the-Lake around Four Mile Creek, with heavy clay-loam soils and about 1,582 growing degree days; warm, early-ripening sites for Cabernet Franc, Merlot and icewine Vidal.

ca-fraser-valley.name: Fraser Valley
ca-fraser-valley.grapes: Pinot Gris, Bacchus, Pinot Noir, Siegerrebe
ca-fraser-valley.summary: A coastal GI in the lower Fraser River valley east of Vancouver, with a wet, mild climate; mostly early-ripening whites and Pinot Noir, and many wineries using Okanagan grapes.

ca-golden-mile-bench.name: Golden Mile Bench
ca-golden-mile-bench.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer
ca-golden-mile-bench.summary: BC's first sub-GI (2015), a 21 km-long, east-facing glacial bench and alluvial fans on the west side of the valley south of Oliver. Gravelly, well-drained soils and morning sun give ripe yet fresh Bordeaux varieties, Syrah and aromatic whites. The name dates from the gold rush at Fairview in the 1890s.

ca-golden-mile-slopes.name: Golden Mile Slopes
ca-golden-mile-slopes.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Gris
ca-golden-mile-slopes.summary: A sub-GI covering the steeper slopes and higher ground above the Golden Mile Bench west of Oliver, with shallower, rockier soils and later afternoon shade; Bordeaux varieties, Syrah and whites.

ca-gulf-islands.name: Gulf Islands
ca-gulf-islands.summary: A coastal GI covering the islands between Vancouver Island and the mainland (Salt Spring, Pender, Saturna), in the rain shadow of the Olympic and Vancouver Island mountains; small producers of Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

ca-kootenays.name: Kootenays
ca-kootenays.summary: A GI (2018) in the mountain valleys of southeastern BC, chiefly the Creston Valley, a warm pocket near the US border; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

ca-lake-country.name: Lake Country
ca-lake-country.grapes: Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay
ca-lake-country.summary: The northernmost Okanagan sub-GI (2022), about 2,500 ha around Winfield and Oyama between Kelowna and Vernon. Cool and lake-moderated; Pinot Noir, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and sparkling. George and Trudy Heiss planted Gray Monk's vineyard in 1972 and pioneered German and Alsace varieties here.

ca-lake-erie-north-shore.name: Lake Erie North Shore
ca-lake-erie-north-shore.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Riesling, Chardonnay, Vidal
ca-lake-erie-north-shore.summary: Ontario's southernmost and warmest mainland appellation, a bow-shaped strip along Lake Erie from Amherstburg to near St. Thomas at about 42 degrees north. Shallow Lake Erie warms quickly, giving more growing degree days than any other Ontario region; red Bordeaux varieties ripen well. Colio Estate (1980) at Harrow is the oldest modern winery; about 15 wineries.

ca-lillooet.name: Lillooet
ca-lillooet.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Riesling
ca-lillooet.summary: A GI (2018) in the Fraser Canyon around Lillooet, a hot, dry rain-shadow pocket with long summer days; a handful of wineries such as Fort Berens grow Bordeaux varieties and Riesling.

ca-lincoln-lakeshore.name: Lincoln Lakeshore
ca-lincoln-lakeshore.summary: A flat, lake-cooled sub-appellation along Lake Ontario in the Town of Lincoln, with a long frost-free season (about 198 days) but cooler summers (about 1,527 growing degree days); it supplies grapes to many Niagara wineries.

ca-naramata-bench.name: Naramata Bench
ca-naramata-bench.grapes: Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay
ca-naramata-bench.summary: A sub-GI (2019) along the east shore of Okanagan Lake north of Penticton, with about 40 wineries on west-facing glacial benches and silt bluffs above the lake. Lake reflection and evening warmth suit Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah and aromatic whites; it is one of BC's most visited wine roads.

ca-niagara-escarpment.name: Niagara Escarpment
ca-niagara-escarpment.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Gamay
ca-niagara-escarpment.summary: A regional appellation joining the three bench sub-appellations (Short Hills, Twenty Mile, Beamsville) along the escarpment between St. Catharines and Grimsby, with 25 wineries. Fossil-rich limestone and dolomite soils, slopes and lake breezes give Ontario's most mineral Riesling and Chardonnay. Not to be confused with the US Niagara Escarpment AVA across the river in New York.

ca-niagara-lakeshore.name: Niagara Lakeshore
ca-niagara-lakeshore.summary: Sub-appellation on the shore of Lake Ontario around the town of Niagara-on-the-Lake, with the longest frost-free season in Niagara (about 213 days) and around 1,563 growing degree days; lake breezes keep it frost-free late into autumn.

ca-niagara-on-the-lake.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
ca-niagara-on-the-lake.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Riesling, Vidal
ca-niagara-on-the-lake.summary: A regional appellation covering the plain below the escarpment between St. Catharines and the Niagara River, with four sub-appellations. It is the warmest, most-visited part of Niagara (39 wineries, about 1,597 growing degree days) and the heartland of Ontario icewine and Bordeaux reds.

ca-niagara-peninsula.name: Niagara Peninsula
ca-niagara-peninsula.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Gamay, Vidal
ca-niagara-peninsula.summary:
Canada's largest appellation and the source of most Ontario VQA wine: 13,600 acres and 105 wineries in 2024 to 2025. The Niagara Escarpment and Lake Ontario create a protected corridor where over 40 varieties ripen. Benchland vineyards along the escarpment give the most structured Riesling and Chardonnay; the warmer lake plain gives Cabernet Franc, Merlot and much of Ontario's icewine.

The Niagara Escarpment, a limestone ridge that runs from New York to Wisconsin and is a UNESCO biosphere reserve in Ontario, is the key to the appellation. Air off Lake Ontario hits the escarpment and circulates back, so the benches stay a few degrees warmer on cold winter nights and cooler in summer heat. Even so, deep freezes (as in the polar-vortex winters of 2014 and 2015) can kill buds, so growers bury graft unions, run wind machines and plant hardy varieties. Niagara's best Chardonnay and Riesling are among the finest cool-climate wines in North America.

ca-niagara-river.name: Niagara River
ca-niagara-river.summary: Sub-appellation (Niagara-on-the-Lake) along the Niagara River, where the deep, fast-moving river carries warm air and keeps frost away; about 1,606 growing degree days and 199 frost-free days. Warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot as well as icewine.

ca-okanagan-falls.name: Okanagan Falls
ca-okanagan-falls.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Syrah
ca-okanagan-falls.summary: A sub-GI (2018) around the town of Okanagan Falls between Skaha and Vaseux lakes, with a varied mix of benches, granitic slopes and glacial lake sediments. Blue Mountain's Pinot Noir and sparkling wines made its name.

ca-okanagan-valley.name: Okanagan Valley
ca-okanagan-valley.grapes: Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling
ca-okanagan-valley.summary:
BC's dominant GI, with about 90 percent of the province's vineyards along 175 km of glacial lakes. It runs from the semi-desert around Osoyoos and Oliver, the warmest place in Canada for grapes, to cooler Kelowna and Lake Country. Bordeaux varieties and Syrah dominate the south; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and sparkling the north. Eleven sub-GIs (2015 to 2022) mark out its benches and slopes.

The valley's north-south axis and its chain of lakes create a steep climate gradient: the desert floor around Osoyoos is among the hottest vineyard land in Canada, while Lake Country, about 175 km north, is much cooler and suited to Riesling and sparkling wine. Long summer days at 49 to 50 degrees north give extra ripening hours, and cold nights keep acidity. The frosts of 2022 and 2024 forced many growers to rethink varieties, with more cold-hardy clones and the replanting of almost all damaged blocks by 2026.

ca-prince-edward-county.name: Prince Edward County
ca-prince-edward-county.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Cabernet Franc
ca-prince-edward-county.summary:
Ontario's newest and coolest primary appellation (2007), an island-like county in Lake Ontario east of Toronto. Shallow clay loam over fractured Trenton limestone drew winemakers looking for Burgundian conditions; the downside is winter cold so severe that many growers bury their vines under soil each autumn and dig them out in spring. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are taut, mineral and low in alcohol; Norman Hardie, Closson Chase, Hinterland (sparkling) and Rosehall Run are leading names.

Burying vines is labour-intensive: in late autumn, growers prune and lay canes in a trench and cover them with soil, then uncover them in spring. That helps them survive winter lows that can fall below minus 25 degrees Celsius. The County has a few dozen wineries, many of them small and family-run, and its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay have drawn comparisons to Burgundy's cooler villages.

ca-short-hills-bench.name: Short Hills Bench
ca-short-hills-bench.summary: The easternmost escarpment bench, a hilly area southwest of St. Catharines around Twelve Mile Creek; relatively far from the lake, it has hot summers but fewer frost-free days (about 187). Henry of Pelham's family estate dates to a land grant of 1794.

ca-shuswap.name: Shuswap
ca-shuswap.grapes: Siegerrebe, Ortega, Pinot Noir, Maréchal Foch
ca-shuswap.summary: A GI (2018) around Shuswap Lake and Salmon Arm, north of the Okanagan, cooler and wetter, with a short season. Growers favour early-ripening vinifera such as Siegerrebe and Ortega and cold-hardy hybrids; Larch Hills claims one of the highest-elevation vineyards in BC.

ca-similkameen-valley.name: Similkameen Valley
ca-similkameen-valley.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Riesling, Chardonnay
ca-similkameen-valley.summary: A narrow, hot valley GI west of the Okanagan around Cawston and Keremeos, walled by rock cliffs that radiate heat, with strong winds that keep disease low. It is known as Canada's organic farming capital; Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Riesling.

ca-skaha-bench.name: Skaha Bench
ca-skaha-bench.summary: A sub-GI (2019) on the east side of Skaha Lake south of Penticton: a steep, west-facing bench of glacial silt, sand and gravel that catches afternoon sun reflected off the lake. Painted Rock's Bordeaux blends and Syrahs are the benchmark.

ca-south-islands.name: South Islands
ca-south-islands.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Vidal
ca-south-islands.summary: A sub-appellation (July 2015) covering the nine islands of the Township of Pelee in Lake Erie, at Canada's southernmost point. Grapes grow mainly on Pelee Island, about 20 km offshore, where the growing season can be 30 days longer than on the mainland and harvest begins in August. Vin Villa, Canada's first commercial winery, opened here in 1866; Pelee Island Winery farms the island's vineyards on sandy loam and clay over limestone.

ca-south-kelowna-slopes.name: South Kelowna Slopes
ca-south-kelowna-slopes.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 800 ha on the slopes above the east side of Okanagan Lake south of Kelowna, home to historic vineyards such as CedarCreek and St. Hubertus; cool, lake-moderated Pinot Noir and Riesling.

ca-st-davids-bench.name: St. David's Bench
ca-st-davids-bench.summary: A raised bench at the foot of the escarpment around St. Davids, with the highest heat accumulation in Niagara (about 1,637 growing degree days); well-drained, sloping soils over the escarpment's lower terrace. Château des Charmes's château stands here.

ca-summerland-bench.name: Summerland Bench
ca-summerland-bench.summary: A sub-GI (2022) on the bench above the town of Summerland, with about 60 ha of vineyards and gentle, sunny slopes of glacial silt; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites.

ca-summerland-lakefront.name: Summerland Lakefront
ca-summerland-lakefront.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling
ca-summerland-lakefront.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 805 ha along the Okanagan Lake shoreline at Summerland, including Trout Creek, where the lake keeps temperatures mild; Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling.

ca-summerland-valleys.name: Summerland Valleys
ca-summerland-valleys.summary: A sub-GI (2022) of about 1,350 ha in the side valleys west of Summerland, including Prairie Valley and Garnet Valley, higher and cooler than the lakeshore. Orchards share the land with vines; cooler nights suit Pinot Noir and aromatic whites.

ca-thompson-valley.name: Thompson Valley
ca-thompson-valley.summary: A GI (2018) around Kamloops on the Thompson River, semi-arid with cold winters, where growers favour hardier varieties and site selection on slopes above the frost-prone valley floor.

ca-tidal-bay.name: Tidal Bay
ca-tidal-bay.grapes: L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Geisenheim 318, Ortega, Chardonnay
ca-tidal-bay.summary: Nova Scotia's appellation-style designation, created by the province's wineries in 2011 with a first vintage in 2012. Tidal Bay is a crisp, aromatic, low-alcohol white blend that must be at least 51 percent L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval Blanc, Vidal and Geisenheim 318 (with 16 other varieties allowed), made from 100 percent Nova Scotia grapes and approved by a blind-tasting panel. It is meant to taste of the sea air of the Bay of Fundy and to pair with local scallops and lobster.

ca-twenty-mile-bench.name: Twenty Mile Bench
ca-twenty-mile-bench.summary: A bench sub-appellation around Jordan and Vineland, cut by Twenty Mile Creek ravines, with steep, limestone-rich slopes and cooling breezes (about 1,523 growing degree days). Home of Cave Spring (1986) and Tawse and some of Ontario's best Riesling and Chardonnay.

ca-vancouver-island.name: Vancouver Island
ca-vancouver-island.grapes: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega, Chardonnay
ca-vancouver-island.summary: A coastal GI covering the island's southeast, sheltered from Pacific storms by the island's mountains. Cool and sunny in summer; Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Ortega and sparkling. Cowichan Valley is its sub-GI.

ca-vin-de-glace-du-quebec.name: Vin de glace du Québec
ca-vin-de-glace-du-quebec.summary: Quebec's IGP for icewine, from grapes (mostly Vidal) frozen naturally on the vine and pressed while frozen, so only concentrated, sugar-rich juice runs off. Quebec's severe winters make icewine a natural speciality, sold alongside the province's ice cider.

ca-vin-du-quebec.name: Vin du Québec
ca-vin-du-quebec.grapes: Frontenac, Marquette, Vidal, Seyval Blanc, Vandal-Cliche, Sainte-Croix
ca-vin-du-quebec.summary: Quebec's protected geographical indication for wine (IGP), requiring 100 percent Quebec-grown grapes, independent certification and production standards; it covers still, sparkling, fortified and late-harvest wines from hybrids and vinifera. Most IGP wines come from Montérégie and the Eastern Townships around Dunham.

ca-vinemount-ridge.name: Vinemount Ridge
ca-vinemount-ridge.summary: The highest and coolest Niagara sub-appellation, on the top ridge of the escarpment above the benches, with the shortest frost-free season (about 178 days) and lowest heat (about 1,469 growing degree days). Riesling and icewine thrive; cold winters are a risk.

sites.name: Inniskillin
sites.text: Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser received Ontario's first new winery licence since 1929 in 1975 and moved to the Brae Burn Estate in 1978. Their 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo 1991, putting Canadian icewine on the world map.

sites.name: Château des Charmes
sites.text: Paul Bosc, an Algerian-born Frenchman, planted Niagara's first large all-vinifera vineyard in 1978 when experts said it could not survive. The family's French-style château stands on St. David's Bench.

sites.name: Cave Spring Cellars
sites.text: Len Pennachetti and Angelo Pavan founded Cave Spring in 1986 in an 1870s apple warehouse in the village of Jordan; their Riesling and Chardonnay from Beamsville Bench and Twenty Mile Bench vineyards helped define bench terroir.

sites.name: Tawse Winery
sites.text: Moray Tawse's gravity-flow, organic and biodynamic winery near Vineland; it was named Canadian Winery of the Year several times and is known for Burgundian Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Pelee Island Winery
sites.text: Pelee Island Winery farms Canada's southernmost vineyards on Pelee Island, with its main winery at Kingsville on the mainland; it made Ontario's first successful icewine in 1983 (50 bottles).

sites.name: Vin Villa ruins, Pelee Island
sites.text: Kentucky planters Thaddeus Smith and Edward and William McCormick founded Vin Villa in 1866, Canada's first commercial winery, on Lake Erie's Pelee Island. Only stone ruins remain.

sites.name: Johann Schiller's Credit River vineyard (Cooksville)
sites.text: Around 1811, Johann Schiller, a German-born former corporal, made wine here from wild and cultivated vines; he is remembered as the father of Canadian wine. The site later became Clair House Vineyards. Today it is suburban Mississauga.

sites.name: Norman Hardie Winery
sites.text: Sommelier-turned-winemaker Norman Hardie planted on Prince Edward County's shallow clay over limestone in 2003 and showed that the County could make taut, low-alcohol, Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. His vines, like most in the County, are buried under soil every winter.

sites.name: Closson Chase
sites.text: A purple barn turned winery, founded in 1998 by a group including film-maker Deborah Paskus, among the first to plant Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in the County.

sites.name: Father Pandosy Mission
sites.text: Oblate missionary Charles Pandosy founded this mission in 1859 and planted the Okanagan's first vines for sacramental wine. Several original log buildings survive as a heritage site in Kelowna.

sites.name: Mission Hill Family Estate
sites.text: Anthony von Mandl's hilltop winery above West Kelowna, rebuilt in 2002 with a 12-storey bell tower; its 1992 Chardonnay won a major award at the International Wine & Spirit Competition in London in 1994, a turning point for BC wine.

sites.name: Quails' Gate
sites.text: The Stewart family, among the Okanagan's pioneer farmers, planted grapes on the west shore of Okanagan Lake in the 1950s and 1960s and founded the winery in 1989; known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Chasselas.

sites.name: Nk'Mip Cellars
sites.text: Opened in 2002 by the Osoyoos Indian Band in partnership with Vincor, Nk'Mip (pronounced 'in-ka-meep') is widely described as the first Indigenous-owned and operated winery in North America, in the desert near Osoyoos.

sites.name: Burrowing Owl Estate (Black Sage Bench)
sites.text: Jim Wyse founded Burrowing Owl on the hot, sandy Black Sage Bench south of Oliver in 1997; its Merlots and Bordeaux blends helped define the south Okanagan style. Part of its proceeds supported the recovery of the endangered burrowing owl.

sites.name: Painted Rock Estate
sites.text: John Skinner planted a former apricot orchard on Skaha Bench in 2004; his Red Icon and Syrah were key evidence for the Skaha Bench sub-GI.

sites.name: Blue Mountain Vineyard and Cellars
sites.text: The Mavety family, growers since 1971, founded this winery in 1991; its traditional-method sparkling wines and Pinot Noir from estate vines anchor the Okanagan Falls sub-GI.

sites.name: Vignoble de l'Orpailleur
sites.text: Founded at Dunham in 1982 by Hervé Durand, Charles-Henri de Coussergues and partners, one of Quebec's first commercial wineries; it showed that Seyval Blanc and hilled-up vines could survive Quebec winters, and houses a wine museum.

sites.name: Domaine des Côtes d'Ardoise
sites.text: Planted in 1980 by Christian Barthomeuf on slate slopes at Dunham, often cited as the first commercial vineyard of modern Quebec. Barthomeuf later invented ice cider.

sites.name: Domaine Pinnacle
sites.text: An orchard estate at Frelighsburg on the slopes of Pinnacle Mountain near the Vermont border, founded in 2000; its ice cider brought the Quebec invention to international markets.

sites.name: Benjamin Bridge
sites.text: Gerry McConnell and Dara Gordon planted vines in the Gaspereau Valley in 2002 with consultant Peter J. Gamble and Champagne-trained advisers; its long-aged traditional-method sparkling wines and Nova 7 put Nova Scotia on the world map.

sites.name: Domaine de Grand Pré
sites.text: Roger Dial opened Nova Scotia's first modern commercial winery here in 1979, beside the UNESCO-listed Acadian dykelands of Grand-Pré, reclaimed from the Bay of Fundy tides in the 1680s. Hanspeter Stutz bought it in 1993; it grows L'Acadie Blanc, Seyval and New York Muscat.

sites.name: L'Acadie Vineyards
sites.text: Bruce Ewert, who had made wine in British Columbia, founded this certified-organic winery in the Gaspereau Valley in 2004. It focuses on long-aged traditional-method sparkling wine from L'Acadie Blanc and on dried-grape (appassimento-style) reds that concentrate flavour in a cool climate.

sites.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
sites.text: The Norse site at the northern tip of Newfoundland (about 1000 AD), the only confirmed Viking settlement in the Americas. Sagas called the land the Norse reached Vinland for its wild grapes; butternuts found here show the Norse travelled south to where grapes grew.
